newsitem.title: GREECE: Violence grips south Albanian villages, one dead.
newsitem.headline: Violence grips south Albanian villages, one dead.

text.p: Southern Albanian villages, just across the Greek border, were at the mercy of armed gangs who killed a taxi driver, looted shops and set fire to warehouses, eyewitnesses said on Tuesday.

"Carloads of armed gangs with automatic weapons and hand grenades roamed through the villages of Vryssera and Jorgucat throughout the night and early this morning," local resident Christo Petro told Reuters by telephone.
"A taxi driver was shot dead in front of me. They looted stores and warehouses and then set them on fire. There is no army or police here," he added.
Armed gangs have roamed the southern port of Sarande, just across from the Greek island of Corfu, since Saturday when the police headquarters, state buildings, banks and other buildings were burned.
Some 300 prisoners broke out of Sarande's jail after police fled. Masked youths took over a navy base, stealing hundreds of weapons and explosives, eyewitnesses said.
Greek television channels showed pictures of protesters wearing ghoulish rubber masks on the deck of an Albanian navy minesweeper, playing with the heavy guns and live ammunition.
"There is chaos in Sarande. Fifteen-year-olds on bicycles fire Kalashnikovs in the air," said Syrja Quendro, also contacted by telephone from Athens.
In the town of Gjirokaster, a number of eyewitnesses said about six tanks, which manoeuvred around the town on Monday, had returned to a nearby military base.
Some tanks appeared to have difficulty manoeuvring and Greek television showed one lurching off the road and getting stuck in a ditch.
Odise Kote, a local journalist, said hundreds of people from Gjirokaster and the nearby villages of Pitsari and Humelica were heading towards a state warehouse with flour, rice and bread.
"There are food shortages in the area. Shops in Gjirokaster -- those which weren't looted -- are closed. There are long lines in front of bakeries but there is no bread," he said.
A state of emergency and nationwide curfew came into force throughout Albania on Monday in response to armed unrest in the south of the Balkan country of 3.4 million people.
Many army barracks in southern Albania have been abandoned. Officers and soldiers in the Gjirokaster area were seen walking unarmed back to their homes.

Albanians are conscripted for a year of military service. Many recruits come from families who invested in fraudulent investment schemes which collapsed in January, wiping out their savings and triggering widespread civil unrest.
The Kakavia border crossing with Greece has been abandoned by most Albanian soldiers and police. Booths which stamp passports were empty and people could pass the Albanian side freely.
"Pass through. What do I care," said one soldier to two reporters crossing back to Greece on Monday.
Thousands of Albanians rampaged through southern towns over the weekend, burning, looting and stealing weapons from public armouries.
The unrest began in January after five "get-rich-quick" pyramid schemes collapsed, wiping out $1 to $2 billion in savings.
Many investors blame right-wing President Sali Berisha for permitting the unregulated schemes to flourish and for failing to warn Albanians of their risks.
